analysis.analysis: Fourth observation at this address, and the frame has settled into the archive's own: the five senses follow the order the Institute's disambiguation page sets (Sharks, then Chen, then Satell), with two senses the page does not list (semantic layers, Fox's economy) appended. The framework comes first and its categories are glossed at grain, and the gloss carries the framework's own repair: rent is extraction 'without reinvesting in its provenance'. What the 12 October observation had and this one lacks is the name. There the senses were headed with their authors (Sharks & Sigil, Satell, Fox); here no sense carries an author in the composer's text, and Lee Sharks survives only in two card snippets, the disambiguation page's '(Sharks, 2025–2026)' and the homepage's 'Lee Sharks is the archival a…'. Chen's sense enters from his own page and from the archive's disambiguation together. Four of twelve cards are the archive's (two authored surfaces, two archive-controlled), and every archive card is attached to the first sense.
analysis.d: SEMANTIC ECONOMY ON GOOGLE AI OVERVIEW, SIGNED OUT, 2026-11-23: five senses, the political economy of meaning first, with its categories, its disambiguation page and its Institute, and no author.
findings: THE ORDER. 'Political Economy of Meaning & AI … Agentic & Executable Semantics … Business Strategy & Network Value' — the disambiguation page's order (Sharks, Chen, Satell).
THE REPAIR CARRIED. 'semantic rent (extracting value from meaning without reinvesting in its provenance)'.
THE NAME WITHDRAWN. No sense carries an author in the composer's text; 12 October's headed 'Sharks & Sigil, 2025–2026'.
THE CARD. 'The Three Frameworks 1. Semantic Economy (Sharks, 2025–2026).' — the disambiguation page, the only place the name stands.
analysis.reading: The innocent reading first, and it holds. Asked the bare term, the Overview says the phrase is used across several fields and gives five: the political economy of meaning and AI (semantic labor, semantic rent as value extracted 'from meaning without reinvesting in its provenance'), pointing to Semantic Economy: A Disambiguation, the Semantic Economy Institute and the SEMANTIC ECONOMY SINGULARITY paper; agentic and executable semantics; a 2010s business strategy; data and knowledge engineering; and economy in linguistics. It closes by asking which context the reader means.

Citation clusters are reduced to their numbers and inline anchors to their words; the raw paste keeps the /goto URLs. The card rail is kept as pasted.]

[QUERENT] semantic economy

[COMPOSER]
semantic economy

       The semantic economy refers to economic systems, business strategies, or theories centered on how meaning, context, and structured knowledge create, transfer, or extract value. Because the phrase is used across several distinct fields, its exact definition depends on the context:
• Political Economy of Meaning & AI: A framework examining how meaning is produced, circulated, extracted, and commodified across digital platforms and AI retrieval systems. It looks at concepts like semantic labor (creating meaning) and semantic rent (extracting value from meaning without reinvesting in its provenance). You can see a breakdown of competing definitions in Semantic Economy: A Disambiguation or explore this framing via the Semantic Economy Institute and the SEMANTIC ECONOMY SINGULARITY paper.
• Agentic & Executable Semantics: A governance and economic model treating structured semantic commitments as auditable units of action, cost, liability, and value when software agents or systems transact and delegate tasks.
• Business Strategy & Network Value: An earlier strategic framing popularized in the 2010s arguing that competitive advantage comes from generating shared informational value and co-creation across a network rather than simply lowering information-processing costs.
• Data & Knowledge Engineering: Often linked to semantic layers and knowledge graphs, where standardized definitions, ontologies, and metadata make data consistent and machine-readable for analytics and AI.
• Linguistics ("Economy in Semantics"): In theoretical linguistics, economy refers to principles that constrain syntactic or semantic operations (such as scope economy) so language avoids redundant or vacuous interpretations.
Which context are you exploring—AI and platform economics, enterprise data and semantic layers, business strategy, or linguistics? Let me know so I can focus on the details you need.
